accroche: Bread nourished yesterday: nothing, David Hume argued in 1748, logically guarantees that it will nourish again tomorrow.
contenu_vulgarise:
A baker has sold bread for twenty years without ever poisoning anyone. No one hesitates, walking into the shop tomorrow, to believe the same will hold. David Hume, in 1748, in *An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding* (Section IV), asks exactly what this confidence rests on, and his answer disappoints: on nothing reason can defend.

## The dilemma

Every inference of this kind, Hume notes, assumes a principle he calls the uniformity of nature: cases not yet observed will resemble those already observed. How can this principle itself be proven? According to Hume, only two kinds of argument are possible: demonstration, and probable reasoning grounded in experience.

Demonstration fails outright: denying that nature stays uniform involves no logical contradiction, nothing prevents conceiving, without contradiction, a world where bread would suddenly start poisoning people. Hume says as much of his own example: that the sun will not rise tomorrow is no less intelligible a proposition, and implies no more contradiction, than the claim that it will rise. What remains is probable reasoning, grounded in the fact that nature has been uniform so far. But relying on past experience to guarantee future experience already assumes that the past informs the future, that is, it assumes the very uniformity of nature it is meant to prove. Hume states it plainly: such an argument “must be evidently going in a circle, and taking that for granted, which is the very point in question.”

## What this shifts

Hume does not conclude that one should stop expecting bread to nourish. He concludes that this expectation owes nothing to reason: it is habit, he says, that carries us there, once the mind has seen two events follow one another often enough. He sees no flaw to correct in it: at the start of Section V, he makes habit the great guide of human life, the one principle that makes our experience useful to us. The shift reaches well beyond the bakery: every inference from observed cases to unobserved ones rests on the same leap from the known to the unknown, with no logical demonstration behind it. The problem has stayed open. Contemporary authors such as Okasha and Norton propose escaping the circularity by denying that all inductive inferences rest on a single uniformity principle, and the discussion continues.

carte.punch: Nothing, Hume argued in 1748, logically proves that tomorrow will resemble yesterday.
carte.idee: In 1748, David Hume shows that no logical demonstration guarantees that the future will resemble the past: proving it through experience would already assume what it sets out to establish. It is habit, not reason, that makes us believe bread will nourish us again tomorrow.

quiz.question: Why, according to Hume, can reasoning based on past experience not prove that the future will resemble the past?
choix: Because no past experience has ever been numerous enough to be convincing
Because such reasoning must already assume that nature is uniform, which is exactly what needs to be proven
Because the formal logic of his time forbade any reasoning about the future
Because only the experimental sciences, not philosophy, can settle this question
quiz.explication: Hume does not question the number of observations, nor does he claim that logic forbids reasoning about the future, and he does not hand the question over to the sciences alone either. His argument is precise: grounding confidence in the future on past experience amounts to taking for granted the very principle that would need to be demonstrated, the uniformity of nature.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Hume, why does the argument from demonstration fail to prove the uniformity of nature?
choix: Because no philosopher before him had attempted this demonstration
Because demonstration requires already knowing the future in advance
Because denying this uniformity involves no logical contradiction
Because only experience, never logic, can demonstrate a fact
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Hume writes that conceiving a world where nature stopped being uniform, where the sun would not rise tomorrow for instance, involves no logical contradiction: nothing in pure demonstration rules out that possibility.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Hume conclude about what makes us believe bread will nourish us again tomorrow?
choix: It is habit, not reason, that produces this belief
It is a scientific law already proven in the eighteenth century
It is a religious certainty, in his view, specific to his era
It is an instinct identical in all animals and in humans
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Hume concludes that reason does not support this expectation: it is habit, born from repeatedly seeing the same events follow one another, that carries us there, and he makes it the great guide of human life.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How do contemporary authors such as Okasha or Norton, per the entry, approach Hume's circularity?
choix: They accept Hume's conclusion and give up on induction altogether
They show that Hume was mistaken about the definition of logic
They replace the uniformity of nature with a single mathematical law
They deny that all inductive inferences rest on one same uniformity principle
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry notes that Okasha and Norton try to escape the circularity by denying that all inductive inferences rest on one single uniformity principle of nature, rather than by refuting Hume outright.
